title: Mental Capacity Act: principles and assessing capacity
blurb: Apply the five MCA principles and the decision-specific capacity test, including fluctuating capacity and age limits.
question: Mrs Dawson, 84, has Alzheimer's disease. She tells the nurse she wants to go home today rather than to a care home. A relative says, "She has dementia, so she can't decide." What is the correct approach?

teach.h: Capacity is the starting point, not the exception
teach.body: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales) protects people who may lack capacity while protecting everyone's right to decide for themselves. Legally, a person lacks capacity for a matter if, at the material time, they are unable to make a decision for themselves because of an impairment of, or a disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain (s2(1)). In plain English: can this person make THIS decision NOW, and if not, is that because of how their mind or brain is working?

head: s1
Principle
rows: Assume capacity unless it is established that the person lacks it
Take all practicable steps to help before deciding they can't
An unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity
Anything done for a person lacking capacity must be in their best interests
Consider whether a less restrictive option would achieve the purpose

letters.word: Use or weigh it to reach a decision
Communicate the decision by any means

teach.caption: Failing any ONE of the four means the person cannot make that decision at that time.

teach.body: Capacity is about a specific matter at the material time (s2(1)). Someone may lack capacity to manage complex investments but be well able to choose lunch. Impairment may be permanent or temporary (s2(2)), so capacity can fluctuate with delirium, infection or encephalopathy. If a decision can wait, choose the time when the person is at their best: that is one of the practicable steps s1(3) requires.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Dawson wants to go home
teach.body: Mrs Dawson's diagnosis does not answer the question. s2(3) says lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a person's condition. The nurse presumes capacity (s1(2)), gives information in a way she can follow, and the decision maker assesses whether she can understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate the information about where to live. If she can, her choice stands, even if the team thinks it unwise (s1(4)).

rows.label: Diagnosis
values: Can she do U, R, U/W, C?

teach.caption: s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by age, appearance, condition or behaviour. s3(3): retaining for a short period is enough.

items: Explain in a way suited to the person: simple language, visual aids, one point at a time.
Use communication aids or speech and language therapy for aphasia; any means of communication counts.
Pick the best time and place: when alert, quiet, after pain relief, with hearing aids in.
Involve people who know how the person communicates.

teach.text: Age 16, not 18: most MCA powers apply from 16 (s2(5)), though advance decisions and LPAs need 18. And the MCA is the law in England and WALES only: Scotland uses the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 and Northern Ireland the Mental Capacity Act (NI) 2016 (Code 4.3).

items: Five principles: presume capacity, help first, unwise is not incapable, best interests, less restrictive.
Test: unable to understand, retain, use or weigh, or communicate, because of mind or brain impairment.
Decision-specific and time-specific; capacity can fluctuate; choose the best time.
Never decide on age, appearance, condition or behaviour alone (s2(3)).
MCA powers apply from 16; Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own capacity law.

summary: You can now apply the five MCA principles, run the four-part functional test for a specific decision at a specific time, and spot the shortcuts (diagnosis, age, unwise choices, short memory) that do not establish incapacity. You also know where the Act applies by age and nation.

A.q: Mrs Dawson, 84, has Alzheimer's disease. She wants to go home rather than to a care home. Her nephew says she cannot decide because of her diagnosis. Which statement is correct?
options: Her capacity for this decision must be assessed, not assumed from diagnosis
Her nephew should decide, as her closest relative involved in her care
She lacks capacity because Alzheimer's is an impairment of the brain
A psychiatrist must formally assess her before anyone can discuss the options
A.why: MCA s1(2): assume capacity unless it is established otherwise; s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a condition. Capacity must be assessed for this decision now.

whyNot.1: A relative has no power to decide for an adult unless appointed (for example as an attorney), and capacity is presumed.
whyNot.2: An impairment is necessary but not sufficient; the person must also be unable to make the decision.
whyNot.3: Capacity is usually assessed by the person proposing the decision; a psychiatrist is not routinely required.

A.q: Mr Pearce, 67, has capacity. After a full explanation he declines a recommended below-knee amputation. The team thinks this is unwise. What does the MCA say?
options: His refusal suggests he cannot weigh up the risks properly
An unwise decision does not by itself mean he lacks capacity
The team should act in his best interests as the risk is high
His family should be asked whether they agree with his choice
A.why: MCA s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because it is unwise. With capacity, his refusal must be respected (Code 2.5).

whyNot.0: Disagreeing with the team is not evidence of being unable to weigh information.
whyNot.2: Best interests decisions apply to people who lack capacity.
whyNot.3: The decision is his; family agreement is not required.

A.q: Mrs Ali, 76, has delirium. She can repeat what the nurse said about a blood transfusion, but cannot see how its benefits and risks apply to her. Which part of the test is she unable to meet?
options: Understanding the relevant information
Retaining the information
Communicating the decision
Using or weighing the information
A.why: MCA s3(1)(c): a person is unable to decide if unable to use or weigh the information as part of the process of making the decision. She understands and retains it but cannot weigh it.

whyNot.0: She can explain what she was told, which shows understanding.
whyNot.1: She can repeat it, so she has retained it.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests she cannot communicate a decision.

B.q: Mr Nowak, 70, has expressive aphasia after a stroke. A decision is needed about moving him to a rehabilitation unit. What should happen before concluding he lacks capacity?
options: Ask his wife what he would have wanted before the stroke
Arrange communication aids or speech and language therapy
Record that he cannot communicate and decide in his best interests
Ask him closed questions and accept a nod as his full decision
B.why: MCA s1(3): not to be treated as unable to decide unless all practicable steps to help have failed; s3(1)(d) allows communication by any means. Aids and SALT support should be tried first.

whyNot.0: Past wishes matter in best interests, which only applies once incapacity is established.
whyNot.2: Concluding incapacity without trying communication support breaches s1(3).
whyNot.3: Closed questions may not show he understands and weighs the options.

B.q: Mr Osei, 80, has mild cognitive impairment. He understands and weighs the discharge options and chooses one, but by the next day he cannot recall the discussion. What is the correct view?
options: He lacks capacity, as he cannot retain information overnight
The decision must be repeated daily until he remembers it
He could make the decision, as brief retention is enough
His family should confirm the choice because he may forget
B.why: MCA s3(3): being able to retain information for a short period only does not prevent a person being regarded as able to make the decision.

whyNot.0: Retention is needed long enough to make the decision, not indefinitely.
whyNot.1: There is no requirement to remember the decision afterwards.
whyNot.3: His decision does not need family confirmation.

B.q: Ms Ruiz, 59, has hepatic encephalopathy. She is drowsy and confused in the evenings but alert most mornings. A non-urgent decision is needed. When is it best to assess her capacity?
options: In the morning, when she is usually at her most alert
In the evening, to see her at her most impaired
Straight away, so the decision is made without delay
After discharge, when the encephalopathy has resolved
B.why: Capacity is time-specific (s2(1)) and s1(3) requires all practicable steps to help the person decide. Choosing her best time supports her to decide herself.

whyNot.1: Assessing at her worst does not give her every chance to decide.
whyNot.2: The decision is non-urgent, so it can wait for her best time.
whyNot.3: The decision is needed while she is an inpatient, and she is often alert enough in the mornings.

C.q: Mr Brennan, 74, was assessed last month as lacking capacity to manage his complex investments. Today he says he would like fish rather than chicken, and wants to sit in the garden. What is the correct approach?
options: Ask his deputy, as he lacks capacity in general
Give him the choices, as capacity is decision-specific
Decide for him in his best interests to keep things simple
Reassess capacity formally before each of these choices
C.why: MCA s2(1): lack of capacity relates to a specific matter at the material time. Being unable to manage complex investments says nothing about everyday choices, which he is presumed able to make (s1(2)).

whyNot.0: There is no such thing as lacking capacity 'in general' under the MCA.
whyNot.2: Best interests decisions only apply where he lacks capacity for that decision.
whyNot.3: Capacity is presumed for each decision unless there is reason to doubt it.

C.q: On a children's ward in England, the nurse is caring for Lily, 15, who needs a decision about a minor procedure. A student asks whether the MCA 2005 applies to Lily. What is the best answer?
options: Yes, the Act applies to everyone receiving NHS care
Yes, if her parents agree that it should be applied
No, its powers generally apply from age 18 onwards
No, its powers generally apply from age 16 onwards
C.why: MCA s2(5): powers under the Act generally do not apply to a person under 16 (subject to s18(3), which concerns property). Lily's consent is considered under Gillick competence and parental responsibility.

whyNot.0: The Act's powers do not generally apply to under-16s.
whyNot.1: Parents cannot extend the Act's powers to a 15-year-old.
whyNot.2: The general threshold is 16; 18 applies to advance decisions and LPAs.

C.q: Mr Achebe, 45, is shouting and refusing a CT scan after a head injury. A colleague says, "He's aggressive, so he obviously lacks capacity." What is the best response?
options: Agree, as aggression shows a disturbance of the mind
Agree, as a recent head injury means he cannot decide now
Explain that behaviour alone cannot establish incapacity
Explain that a doctor must make the capacity judgement
C.why: MCA s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a person's behaviour. His ability to understand, retain, use or weigh and communicate must be assessed (s3).

whyNot.0: Aggression may have many causes and is not in itself proof of incapacity.
whyNot.1: A head injury may cause an impairment, but the functional test still has to be applied.
whyNot.3: The person proposing the act or decision assesses capacity; it does not have to be a doctor.

reteach.title: Two questions: can they, and if not, why not?
reteach.question: How would you explain the capacity test to a relative in two sentences?

blocks.h: Can they, for this decision, right now?
blocks.body: First: with all the help we can give, can the person understand the information, hold it long enough, weigh it up, and tell us their choice in any way? If yes, they decide, even if we disagree. Second, only if they can't: is that because of something affecting how their mind or brain works, such as dementia, delirium or a head injury? A diagnosis on its own never answers the first question.

blocks.text: A capacity judgement is about the PROCESS of deciding, never the OUTCOME the person chooses.

explain.body: Presume capacity; take all practicable steps to help; an unwise decision is not incapacity; act in best interests; choose the less restrictive option (MCA s1(2)-(6)).

test.q: Which MCA principle applies before a person is assessed as unable to make a decision?
options: Act in the person's best interests
Take all practicable steps to help them
Consult the person's next of kin as a first step
Choose the least restrictive option
test.why: s1(3): a person is not treated as unable to decide unless all practicable steps to help have been taken without success.

whyNot.0: Best interests applies after incapacity is established.
whyNot.2: Next of kin have no automatic role in assessing capacity.
whyNot.3: The less restrictive option applies when acting for someone who lacks capacity.

explain.body: Unable to understand, retain, use or weigh, or communicate the information (s3(1)). Brief retention is enough (s3(3)); communication by any means counts.

test.q: A man can explain the risks of surgery but says he will die anyway, so nothing matters, due to severe depression. Which element may be affected?
options: Understanding the information
Retaining the information
Using or weighing the information
Communicating his decision to the team
test.why: He understands the facts, but his depression may stop him using or weighing them in reaching a decision (s3(1)(c)).

whyNot.0: He can explain the risks, showing understanding.
whyNot.1: He has held the information long enough to explain it.
whyNot.3: He is able to express a view.

explain.body: Capacity relates to a specific matter at the material time (s2(1)). Impairment may be temporary (s2(2)). Assess when the person is at their best if the decision can wait.

test.q: A woman with a urinary infection is confused today and may improve with treatment. A non-urgent decision is needed. What is best?
options: Decide today in her best interests
Wait until treatment may have helped
Ask her husband to decide for her
Record that she lacks capacity long-term
test.why: Capacity can be temporary; where the decision can wait, give her the chance to decide herself (s1(3), s2(2)).

whyNot.0: A non-urgent decision should not be made for her if she may soon be able to make it.
whyNot.2: A spouse has no legal power to decide without an LPA or deputyship.
whyNot.3: Her impairment may be temporary, so a long-term conclusion is wrong.

explain.body: Not established by age, appearance, condition or behaviour (s2(3)). Judged on the balance of probabilities (s2(4)). MCA powers generally apply from 16 (s2(5)); England and Wales only.

test.q: What standard of proof applies when deciding whether a person lacks capacity under the MCA?
options: Beyond reasonable doubt
Clear and convincing evidence
Agreement of two professionals
The balance of probabilities
test.why: MCA s2(4): any question whether a person lacks capacity is decided on the balance of probabilities.

whyNot.1: This is not the MCA standard.
whyNot.2: The MCA does not require two professionals to agree.
